findings.summary: SYSTEMIC PATTERN: Tools for Humanity/Worldcoin operates through an offshore IP-stripping structure — patents transferred to Cayman Foundation, token warrants used as securities, placement agent paid in WLD tokens, and $0 disclosed use of proceeds — while collecting biometric iris data that has triggered enforcement in 11+ jurisdictions
findings.detail: Tools for Humanity Corporation raised $115M Series C in April 2023 led by Blockchain Capital. TFH transferred all 6 patents to Worldcoin Foundation (Cayman) in March 2024. FTP Securities LLP paid 600,000 WLD tokens (~$1.56M FMV at $2.60) as placement agent fees. Form D filings report $0 gross proceeds used across all 4 offerings. World Foundation (offshore) controls World Assets Limited. TOOLS FOR HUMANITY LIMITED (Scotland, UK, SC817653) incorporated July 2024, dissolved December 2025 — 17-month lifespan. 11+ international jurisdictions have taken enforcement action for biometric data collection without valid legal basis.

findings.summary: Tools for Humanity raised $115M Series C in April 2023, led by Blockchain Capital; total funding approximately $194M across 3 rounds. Investors include a16z (Andreessen Horowitz), Bain Capital Ventures, Khosla Ventures.
findings.detail: Funding rounds per Tracxn/Crunchbase: Series A (Feb 2021), Series B (Feb 2022), Series C (Apr 2023, $115M, lead: Blockchain Capital). A further $135M was raised from Andreessen Horowitz in 2025 for US network expansion. Reid Hoffman also listed as investor. Sam Altman equity stake not publicly disclosed.

findings.summary: German Bavarian DPA ordered Worldcoin/Tools for Humanity to delete iris codes collected without valid GDPR legal basis by Jan 19, 2025
findings.detail: German regulator ruling Dec 19, 2024: TFH must implement GDPR-compliant deletion procedure, obtain explicit consent for processing activities, and delete previously collected iris codes gathered without sufficient legal basis during 2023. Spain, Hong Kong, Brazil (Jan 2025), South Korea (Sep 2024) also imposed bans or enforcement.

findings.summary: Tools for Humanity launched US Orb operations on May 1, 2025 in six cities (Atlanta, Austin, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, San Francisco) collecting iris biometrics in exchange for WLD cryptocurrency.
findings.detail: Users submit to iris scan via 'Orb' device. Biometric creates 'iris code' stored on blockchain. Company claims images are deleted from Orb within seconds, but consent forms reference data transfer to user phones. Blockchain storage is permanent and irrevocable by company's own disclosure. As of late 2025: ~38.4M World App users, ~17.8M with verified iris scans. Partnerships with Match Group/Tinder, Stripe, Visa, Razer.

findings.summary: Kenya High Court ruled Worldcoin biometric data collection unlawful on May 5, 2025; ordered deletion; Tools for Humanity GmbH confirmed data deleted Jan 2026
findings.detail: Kenya High Court: TFH Corporation and TFH GmbH found liable for breach of right to privacy and Data Protection Act. Consent via cryptocurrency incentive (WLD tokens) ruled invalid. Cross-border data transfers to Cayman Islands and BVI entities found unlawful. ODPC confirmed deletion Jan 2026.

findings.summary: Pro se plaintiff 'Kimmel' filed civil complaint against Tools for Humanity Corporation in D. Colorado (1:25-cv-02151) on July 11, 2025 — ten days after Colorado's biometric Privacy Act amendments took effect.
findings.detail: Case filed July 11, 2025 by pro se plaintiff (IFP). Filed just 10 days after Colorado H.B. 24-1130 biometric amendments to the Colorado Privacy Act took effect July 1, 2025. Judge assigned: Richard T. Gurley. Case caption includes 'et al' suggesting additional defendants beyond TFH. CourtListener docket ID 70769069, PACER ID 245420.

findings.summary: The Kimmel complaint likely alleged violations of Colorado Privacy Act (CPA) biometric provisions (H.B. 24-1130) triggered by TFH's Orb operations and iris scan collection practices.
findings.detail: Colorado's H.B. 24-1130 amended the CPA effective July 1, 2025 to require: (1) written consent before collecting biometric identifiers; (2) prohibition on selling biometric data; (3) destruction requirements. TFH's Orb program — offering cryptocurrency payment for iris scans — is precisely targeted by these provisions. The 10-day gap between law effective date and complaint filing is consistent with a plaintiff who either underwent an Orb scan or reviewed TFH's practices after the law took effect. Complaint text unavailable; this is an inference from circumstantial evidence.

findings.summary: Kimmel v. TFH is the only identified US federal lawsuit against Tools for Humanity or World/Worldcoin as of April 2026. No US class actions filed.
findings.detail: CourtListener RECAP search for 'Tools for Humanity' and 'Worldcoin' across all US federal courts returned only this one case. Web searches for BIPA/biometric class actions against TFH found no results. The company's US operations only launched May 2025, so class action exposure is nascent. Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Colorado CPA, and other state biometric laws all create potential class action exposure for the Orb program.

findings.summary: At least 11 international jurisdictions have taken enforcement action against Tools for Humanity / World / Worldcoin for biometric data privacy violations as of late 2025.
findings.detail: Kenya (May 2025, court ordered permanent data deletion); Colombia (Oct 2025, immediate permanent shutdown ordered by SIC, 5 violations of Law 1581); Philippines (Oct 2025, NPC cease-and-desist); Thailand (Nov 2025, halt + delete 1.2M iris scans); Spain (2024, operations suspended; TFH lawsuit against regulator failed); South Korea (2024, fined 1.1B KRW); Germany/Bavaria (Dec 2024, GDPR deletion order); Brazil (Jan 2025, ban upheld); Hong Kong (2024, violations found); Indonesia (May 2025, suspended); France/UK (investigations 2023-2024). Core regulatory objection in every case: financial incentives compromise consent for biometric data.

findings.summary: Kimmel v. TFH ended with a Judgment on October 28, 2025 — 3.5 months after filing — consistent with IFP screening dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e).
findings.detail: Docket entry 18 is a 'Judgment' filed Oct 28, 2025. Entry 17 on the same day is 'Order AND Order Reassigning Case.' The case was reassigned and closed on the same day. No defense attorney or defendant response appears in the docket. The plaintiff filed In Forma Pauperis twice (Aug 13 and Sep 19) without apparent resolution until dismissal. No RECAP documents are available.
